questions.stem: Compared with Thutmosis III, the reign of Amenhotep III is best described as:
options: long and prosperous, with diplomacy more than war
dominated by yearly campaigns to the Euphrates against Mitanni
a time of famine and civil war between Thebes and Memphis
brief, ending when the Hittites seized the Delta from Egypt
questions.explanation: Amenhotep III ruled for about 38 years at the height of Egypt's wealth, campaigning little and relying on diplomacy and marriage alliances with powers such as Mitanni and Babylon. Thutmosis III, by contrast, led many campaigns into Syria.

questions.stem: A large commemorative scarab of Amenhotep III announces his marriage to Tiye and names her parents, Yuya and Tjuyu, who were not royal. This is significant because it:
options: proves that Tiye's father had been High Priest of Amun at Karnak
openly presented a woman of non-royal birth as Great Royal Wife
shows that Tiye was a Mitannian princess sent to Egypt as a bride
records that Tiye ruled as king after Amenhotep III's death
questions.explanation: Earlier chief queens were usually royal, but Amenhotep III publicised Tiye's non-royal parentage on scarabs sent around Egypt and beyond. Tiye became highly influential, and foreign kings such as Tushratta of Mitanni wrote to her directly; the Mitannian princess in his harem was Gilukhepa.

questions.stem: Amenhotep III's building projects on the west bank at Thebes included:
options: the terraced temple of Djeser-djeseru and the tomb of the Vizier Rekhmire
the Ramesseum and the workers' village built for the royal tomb crew
the Gempaaten and a palace for the worship of the Aten at East Karnak
the Malkata palace and a mortuary temple fronted by the Colossi of Memnon
questions.explanation: Malkata was Amenhotep III's palace complex, where his jubilees were celebrated, and the two colossal seated statues called the Colossi of Memnon stood before his vast mortuary temple. Djeser-djeseru was Hatshepsut's, the Ramesseum was Rameses II's, and the Gempaaten was built by Amenhotep IV on the east bank.

questions.stem: At Karnak and Luxor, Amenhotep III's building included:
options: the talatat temples of the Aten at East Karnak
the Third Pylon at Karnak and much of the temple of Luxor
the Great Hypostyle Hall at Karnak and the Ramesseum
the Akh-menu festival hall and Hatshepsut's obelisks
questions.explanation: Amenhotep III added the Third Pylon at Karnak and built much of Luxor temple for Amun, showing heavy investment in Amun's cult. The Hypostyle Hall came later under Seti I and Rameses II, and the talatat temples were his son's.

questions.stem: Amenhotep III celebrated three Sed festivals in the last decade of his reign. A Sed festival was:
options: a jubilee renewing the king's power, normally first held after 30 years
the yearly festival in which Amun's statue travelled from Karnak to Luxor
a ceremony crowning the king's heir as co-ruler alongside his father
a funeral rite performed by the new king for the king who had died
questions.explanation: The Sed festival renewed the king's strength and divine authority and was usually first celebrated in the thirtieth year of a reign. The journey of Amun from Karnak to Luxor was the Opet Festival, and the funeral rite of the successor was the Opening of the Mouth.

questions.stem: Which evidence best supports the view that the Aten was already prominent before Amenhotep IV came to the throne?
options: Amenhotep III used the epithet ‘the Dazzling Aten’ for himself and his works
Amenhotep III ordered the name of Amun to be erased from temples across Egypt
Amenhotep III built a new capital for the Aten in Middle Egypt
Amenhotep III closed the temples of Amun at Karnak and Luxor
questions.explanation: Amenhotep III's reign shows growing solar emphasis, including the epithet ‘the Dazzling Aten’ used for the king, his palace and a royal barge. The erasure of Amun, the new capital and the attack on Amun's cult all belong to Akhenaten's reign, which is what made it a crisis.

questions.stem: Amenhotep III was worshipped as a living god in his temple at Soleb in Nubia. Historians link this to the Amarna Period because it:
options: shows that Amenhotep III had already abandoned the god Amun
proves that Akhenaten was born and raised at Soleb in Nubia
records the first appearance of the Aten as a sun disk
foreshadows Akhenaten's emphasis on the king's own divinity
questions.explanation: At Soleb, Amenhotep III was shown worshipping a deified form of himself, which suggests an increasing stress on the king's divinity that Akhenaten took further. Amenhotep III still built lavishly for Amun, so Soleb shows continuity as well as change.

questions.stem: Some historians argue that Akhenaten's religious reform was partly political. On this view, his aim was to:
options: hand the government of Egypt to the priests of Ra at Heliopolis
unite Egypt and Mitanni under the worship of a single shared god
reduce the wealth and influence of the priesthood of Amun
win the support of the priests of Amun for a war against the Hittites
questions.explanation: By the late 18th Dynasty the Amun priesthood controlled vast wealth from royal gifts, so redirecting resources to the Aten, whom only the king could serve, reduced their power. Other historians stress Akhenaten's personal religious conviction, so this is an interpretation to be weighed against the evidence.

questions.stem: The talatat used in Amenhotep IV's buildings were:
options: limestone flakes used by scribes for writing everyday notes
small standard-sized sandstone blocks that one man could carry
mud bricks stamped with the name of the Aten and the king
huge granite blocks quarried at Aswan for colossal statues
questions.explanation: Talatat measured roughly one cubit by half a cubit, so they could be handled by one worker and set quickly, letting the Aten temples rise fast. Limestone flakes used for notes are ostraca.

questions.stem: Tens of thousands of decorated talatat from the Aten temples at East Karnak survive today mainly because:
options: Akhenaten buried them in pits when he left Thebes for Akhetaten
Tutankhamun had them moved to his tomb in the Valley of the Kings
they were sent to Mitanni as gifts and found there in the 1800s
later kings used them as fill inside new pylons at Karnak
questions.explanation: After the Amarna Period, kings such as Horemheb dismantled the Aten temples and packed the blocks inside pylons, which protected their reliefs until excavators recovered them. The blocks were reused as fill, not deliberately buried or moved to tombs.

questions.stem: In about his fifth year, Amenhotep IV changed his name to Akhenaten. The change signalled:
options: his marriage to Nefertiti at Karnak
the end of the jubilee for his father
a break with Amun in favour of the Aten
his coronation as king after a co-regency
questions.explanation: Amenhotep means ‘Amun is satisfied’, while Akhenaten means ‘effective for the Aten’, often rendered ‘Spirit of the Aten’. The new name came with the move towards Akhetaten and the exclusive worship of the Aten.

questions.stem: In Amarna art, the Aten is shown as:
options: a falcon-headed man crowned with the double crown
a ram-headed god seated on a throne within a shrine at Karnak
a scarab beetle pushing the sun across the sky
a sun disk whose rays end in hands, some holding the ankh
questions.explanation: The mature Aten was shown only as a disk with rays ending in hands that offer life, the ankh, usually to the king and queen. The ram-headed and scarab forms belonged to Amun and Khepri, the traditional gods Akhenaten turned away from.

questions.stem: The city of Akhetaten, modern Amarna, was built:
options: in the eastern Delta, on the site of the old Hyksos capital Avaris
in Nubia, near the temple of Amenhotep III at Soleb
on an unused site in Middle Egypt, between Thebes and Memphis
on the west bank at Thebes, next to the Valley of the Kings
questions.explanation: Akhetaten, ‘Horizon of the Aten’, was founded on an empty stretch of the east bank in Middle Egypt. It was deliberately away from Thebes, the city of Amun.

questions.stem: According to the boundary stelae, Akhenaten chose the site of Akhetaten because:
options: it lay close to the Hittite border and could be defended
it belonged to no god, goddess or ruler before the Aten
it was the birthplace of his father Amenhotep III and his mother Tiye
the priests of Amun had offered it to the Aten as a gift
questions.explanation: The stelae say the Aten led the king to a place that no god, goddess or ruler owned, and they fix the city's boundaries and the royal burial in the eastern mountain. Choosing virgin land kept the new city free of any other god's claims.

questions.stem: A historian uses the boundary stelae of Akhetaten as evidence. Their main value and limitation are that they:
options: are private letters to foreign kings, so they say little about religion
were carved by workers who opposed the move, so they exaggerate its cost
show the king's intentions as he wished them seen, not how others reacted
record the views of the Amun priests, but were written after Akhenaten died
questions.explanation: The stelae are royal proclamations carved into the cliffs, so they are direct evidence of what Akhenaten wanted to proclaim about the Aten and the city. Because they are official, they reveal nothing directly about how priests, officials or ordinary Egyptians felt.

questions.stem: The Great Hymn to the Aten, found in the tomb of Ay at Amarna, says that no one knows the Aten except the king. This reflects:
options: the custom of officials writing hymns that criticised the king's beliefs
the king's role as the only intermediary between the Aten and people
the priests' belief that the Aten was a secret god of the dead
the hymn's origin in the temple of Amun at Karnak under Amenhotep III
questions.explanation: In Atenism the king and his family alone worshipped the Aten directly, and everyone else approached the god through them. The hymn was carved in an official's tomb to show loyalty, not criticism.

questions.stem: Which idea appears in the Great Hymn to the Aten?
options: the Aten created all lands and peoples, including foreigners
Osiris judges the dead in the Hall of the Two Truths
Amun is king of the gods and the lord of the temple of Karnak at Thebes
the king will be reborn among the never-setting stars
questions.explanation: The hymn praises the Aten as the sole creator who made every land and people and gives life to all creatures. It leaves out Osiris and the traditional afterlife, and Amun has no place in it.

questions.stem: Tomb reliefs of officials at Amarna mostly show:
options: the owner's judgement before Osiris and the weighing of his heart
the owner farming his estates and hunting in the marshes
the owner leading the army against the Hittites in Syria
the royal family worshipping the Aten and rewarding the tomb's owner
questions.explanation: Amarna officials filled their tombs with the king, queen and daughters worshipping the Aten, processing in chariots and rewarding the owner with gold from the Window of Appearance. Traditional Osiris and daily-life scenes largely disappear.

questions.stem: Some historians argue that Akhenaten withdrew from governing Egypt. Why are the Amarna tomb reliefs weak evidence for this view?
options: they were carved by Hittite artists who had never seen the king at work
they show Akhenaten leading his army in person against the Hittites in Syria every year
they were all destroyed by Horemheb, so nothing of them survives today
they show worship and court ceremony, so their silence on government proves little
questions.explanation: The reliefs were designed to honour the king and the Aten, so they naturally show worship, processions and rewards rather than daily administration. The absence of government scenes reflects their purpose, and other evidence, such as officials' titles and a Nubian campaign, shows the state still functioning.

questions.stem: Under Akhenaten, agents travelled through Egypt hacking out the name of Amun from monuments. This shows that the reform:
options: was carried out by Tutankhamun after his father's death
aimed to restore Amun's cult to its place as the state religion
went beyond favouring the Aten to attacking the traditional gods
was carried out only at Akhetaten, leaving Thebes untouched
questions.explanation: The erasures, which sometimes removed even the word ‘gods’, show an active campaign against Amun across Egypt, including Thebes. The restoration of Amun came later, under Tutankhamun.

questions.stem: A house-altar stela shows Akhenaten and Nefertiti playing with their daughters beneath the rays of the Aten. Compared with earlier royal art, this scene is unusual because it:
options: places the queen above the king as the more important ruler
shows the royal family in a strict row of identical profiles
shows the royal family in an informal and affectionate way
shows the king smiting his enemies before the gods of Thebes
questions.explanation: Amarna art showed the royal family kissing and holding their children, intimacy almost absent from earlier royal art. Such stelae stood in private homes, where the royal family under the Aten became a focus of worship.

questions.stem: Some historians once argued that Akhenaten's long face, narrow chest and wide hips in art reflect a medical disorder. One argument against this is that:
options: officials and others at Amarna were also shown with similar features
the king appears in Amarna art only as a falcon-headed human figure
the style was introduced only under Tutankhamun after Akhenaten died
Amarna artists never showed the king's body below the shoulders at all
questions.explanation: If the style recorded an illness, the king's subjects would not share it, yet officials and family members were shown in the same way, and the style softened later in the reign. Many historians therefore read it as religious or artistic symbolism, perhaps of the king as a creator combining male and female.

questions.stem: The Amarna Letters are:
options: limestone ostraca recording the work of the tomb-building crew
inscriptions carved on the boundary stelae around Akhetaten
clay tablets of diplomatic letters written in Akkadian cuneiform
papyrus rolls of temple accounts kept by the priests of the Aten
questions.explanation: The letters, found at Amarna, are cuneiform tablets in Akkadian, the diplomatic language of the time, exchanged between Egypt and the great kings and vassal rulers of the Near East. Most date from the late reign of Amenhotep III and the reign of Akhenaten.

questions.stem: In the Amarna Letters, the king of Mitanni calls the pharaoh ‘my brother’, while the ruler of Byblos calls him ‘my lord’. The difference reflects:
options: Mitanni's status as an equal great power and Byblos's as a vassal
the Mitannian king's position as a relative of the pharaoh's mother
the ruler of Byblos being senior in age to the king of Mitanni
a change of Egyptian policy between the two letters' writing
questions.explanation: Great kings such as those of Mitanni, Babylon, Hatti and Assyria addressed each other as brothers, while vassals in Canaan and Syria wrote as servants to their lord. The terms reflect status in the diplomatic system, not age or family ties.

questions.stem: In his letters to Akhenaten, Tushratta of Mitanni complains that:
options: Egyptian troops had seized his capital and taken his daughters to Egypt as hostages
Akhenaten had refused to marry any princess from the royal house of Mitanni
the Aten's priests had been sent to Mitanni to close the temples of his gods
he received gold-plated wooden statues instead of the solid gold ones promised
questions.explanation: Tushratta reminds Akhenaten that Amenhotep III had promised statues of solid gold and protests that he received gilded wood, and he urges him to ask his mother Tiye. Gold was central to Egyptian diplomacy, so the dispute shows strain in relations with an ally.

questions.stem: Rib-Hadda of Byblos wrote dozens of letters begging Egypt for troops. Why is it risky to use these letters as proof that Akhenaten neglected his empire?
options: vassals exaggerated dangers to win help, and Egypt's replies mostly do not survive
Rib-Hadda wrote them all after Akhenaten died, so they describe Tutankhamun's reign
the letters were forged by Hittite agents to make Egypt appear weak
Byblos was an enemy of Egypt, so its letters are deliberately misleading
questions.explanation: Vassals competed for Egyptian attention and routinely painted their situation as desperate, and the archive holds mainly letters received, not Egypt's answers or actions. The letters show real instability in Syria, but they cannot by themselves prove royal neglect.

questions.stem: During the Amarna Period, Egypt's position in northern Syria was weakened mainly by:
options: the expansion of the Hittites under Suppiluliuma I at Mitanni's expense
an invasion of the Delta by the Sea Peoples and their Libyan allies
the Assyrian conquest of Egypt's Nubian gold mines
a Babylonian army that captured Byblos and Megiddo
questions.explanation: Suppiluliuma I broke the power of Mitanni and drew Syrian states such as Amurru, under Aziru, into the Hittite orbit. The Sea Peoples and Libyans attacked much later, under Merenptah and Rameses III.

questions.stem: Tombs at Amarna show a great reception of foreign delegations bringing tribute in Akhenaten's Year 12, and a campaign in Nubia is recorded in the same period. Historians use this evidence to argue that:
options: the king had not wholly withdrawn from foreign affairs and display of power
Akhenaten had conquered the Hittite kingdom and taken its tribute
the Amarna Letters must all have been written long after Akhenaten's reign ended
Egypt had given up Nubia and moved its gold mines to Syria
questions.explanation: The Year 12 reception and the Nubian campaign show Akhenaten receiving foreign goods and using force, which complicates the picture of a king lost in religion. Egypt never conquered Hatti, and Nubia remained under Egyptian control.

questions.stem: Nefertiti and Akhenaten had:
options: two sons
one son and one daughter
no children
six daughters
questions.explanation: Six daughters of Akhenaten and Nefertiti are known, including Meritaten and Ankhesenpaaten, later Ankhesenamun. No son of Nefertiti is attested.

questions.stem: One theory links Nefertiti's family to Ay. A key piece of evidence is that Ay's wife Tey held the title:
options: nurse of the Great Royal Wife Nefertiti
God's Wife of Amun at Karnak
daughter of Tushratta, the king of Mitanni
First Prophet of the Aten
questions.explanation: Tey is called Nefertiti's nurse, not her mother, which suggests a close family link without proving Ay was her father. Nefertiti's origins remain debated, so the evidence supports a theory rather than a fact.

questions.stem: Historians who reject the theory that Nefertiti was a foreign princess from Mitanni often point out that:
options: her sister Mutnodjmet appears in Amarna tombs, suggesting an Egyptian family
the Amarna Letters name her as the daughter of the king of Babylon
she is shown wearing a foreign Mitannian costume in every Amarna relief of her
her mummy was identified in Tushratta's capital in northern Syria
questions.explanation: Nefertiti's sister appears at court, which fits an Egyptian elite family better than a foreign princess sent as a bride. The Mitannian princesses known from the letters are named Gilukhepa and Tadukhipa, and no source names Nefertiti as foreign-born.

questions.stem: Talatat from Karnak show Nefertiti smiting a captive, an image normally reserved for kings. Historians use such scenes to argue that Nefertiti:
options: led the Egyptian army in person against the Hittites in Syria
had been removed from power and was shown as Egypt's enemy
was worshipped as a goddess of war in place of the Aten
held unusual power and was shown in a role close to kingship
questions.explanation: Nefertiti was shown performing rituals, sometimes without the king, and in the smiting pose of a pharaoh, which suggests an exceptional status. The scene is ideological and does not show her actually commanding troops.

questions.stem: An inscription dated to Year 16 of Akhenaten names Nefertiti as Great Royal Wife. This evidence weakens the theory that:
options: Akhenaten built Akhetaten as a city for the Aten
Nefertiti was shown with the king in Amarna art
Nefertiti died or fell from favour around Year 12 or 14
Nefertiti was the mother of the princess Meritaten
questions.explanation: Nefertiti's apparent disappearance from records after about Year 12 once led historians to assume she had died or been disgraced, but the Year 16 inscription shows her still queen late in the reign. It leaves open whether she then became co-regent or ruled on her own.

questions.stem: The debate about whether Nefertiti became co-regent or ruled alone centres on:
options: the tomb of Nefertiti found intact in the Valley of the Kings
a ruler named Neferneferuaten who appears late in the period
letters from Nefertiti to the Hittite king asking for a son
a statue of Nefertiti wearing the double crown at Karnak
questions.explanation: A ruler called Ankhkheperure Neferneferuaten, sometimes with female forms of titles, appears at the end of Akhenaten's reign, and Neferneferuaten was part of Nefertiti's name. Whether this ruler was Nefertiti, or someone else such as Meritaten, is debated, and Nefertiti's tomb has not been found.

questions.stem: The painted limestone bust of Nefertiti now in Berlin was found in 1912:
options: in the workshop of the sculptor Thutmose at Amarna
in the tomb of Tutankhamun in the Valley of the Kings
inside the Tenth Pylon of the temple of Karnak
in the royal palace of Amenhotep III at Malkata
questions.explanation: A German expedition found the bust in the house and workshop of the sculptor Thutmose at Amarna. It was probably a model for other portraits, which helps explain why it was left behind when the city was abandoned.

questions.stem: The young king Tutankhaten changed his name to Tutankhamun. The change signalled:
options: his adoption by Nefertiti as her son and heir
a new treaty with the Hittite king Suppiluliuma
his move from Memphis to the city of Akhetaten
the restoration of Amun and the traditional gods
questions.explanation: Replacing Aten with Amun in his name, and in his wife's name, marked the return to traditional religion. The court left Akhetaten for Memphis and Thebes; it did not move there.

questions.stem: Tutankhamun's queen, Ankhesenamun, was:
options: a daughter of Akhenaten and Nefertiti, first named Ankhesenpaaten
a Hittite princess sent to Egypt to seal the peace after Kadesh
the daughter of Ay and Tey, who was raised at the court of Mitanni
Tutankhamun's grandmother Tiye, who ruled as regent for him
questions.explanation: Ankhesenpaaten was the third daughter of Akhenaten and Nefertiti, and her name changed to Ankhesenamun with the restoration. Marrying her linked Tutankhamun to the royal line of Akhenaten.

questions.stem: Tutankhamun's Restoration Stela at Karnak says that before his reign:
options: the Nile had failed to flood for seven years because of Akhenaten
the temples had fallen into ruin and the gods had turned away from Egypt
the Hittites had conquered Memphis and carried off the statues of Amun
Nefertiti had ruled as king and abolished the priesthood of the Aten
questions.explanation: The stela describes neglected temples, gods who no longer answered prayers and an army that failed in Syria, then lists Tutankhamun's restoration of temples, cult images and priesthoods. It never names Akhenaten, but its picture is plainly aimed at his reign.

questions.stem: The Restoration Stela was issued in the boy-king Tutankhamun's name and later usurped by Horemheb. A historian should treat its account of the Amarna Period with caution because it:
options: was carved by Akhenaten's supporters and so understates the crisis
was written centuries later by priests who knew little of the period
describes only events in Nubia and does not mention Egypt's temples
was propaganda for the new regime, written to blame the previous reign
questions.explanation: The stela was produced by Tutankhamun's government, probably guided by advisers such as Ay and Horemheb, to justify the restoration by painting the previous reign as a disaster. It is contemporary, but its purpose means it may exaggerate the ruin it describes.

questions.stem: A CT scan of Tutankhamun's mummy in 2005 weakened the theory that he was murdered by a blow to the head, because it found that:
options: the mummy in the tomb was not Tutankhamun's but his successor Ay's
he had died of an arrow wound received in a battle in Syria
his skull had been replaced with a gilded plaster head by the priests
the loose bone fragments in his skull were probably caused after death
questions.explanation: The fragments seen on a 1968 X-ray were found to have been dislodged during embalming or the 1920s examination, not by a fatal blow. Later DNA tests pointed to illness, including malaria, and a leg fracture as more likely factors in his early death.

questions.stem: In Tutankhamun's burial chamber, Ay is painted performing the Opening of the Mouth ceremony on the dead king. Historians see this as:
options: Ay showing himself as the rightful heir who buried his predecessor
evidence that Ay was Tutankhamun's father and had raised him at Thebes
proof that Ay had murdered the king and wished to confess his crime
a scene copied from the tomb of Amenhotep III at the Valley of the Kings
questions.explanation: Performing the burial rites was a duty of the heir, so the scene supports Ay's claim to the throne after Tutankhamun's early death. It shows a ritual role, not parentage or guilt.

questions.stem: A Hittite source, the Deeds of Suppiluliuma, records that a widowed Egyptian queen:
options: asked the Hittite king to send a son for her to marry
invited the Hittites to invade Egypt and remove Horemheb
sent Tutankhamun's gold mask to the Hittite capital
fled to the Hittite court with the daughters of Akhenaten
questions.explanation: The queen wrote that her husband had died and she had no son, and asked for a Hittite prince; Prince Zannanza was sent but died on the way. Which queen wrote the letter is debated, with Ankhesenamun one of the main candidates.

questions.stem: Seti I's king list at Abydos moves straight from Amenhotep III to Horemheb. This shows that:
options: later kings treated the Amarna rulers as illegitimate and erased them
Akhenaten, Tutankhamun and Ay had never actually ruled Egypt
Horemheb was Amenhotep III's son and his direct successor
the list was damaged and the missing names were lost by accident
questions.explanation: Leaving out Akhenaten, Smenkhkare, Tutankhamun and Ay was a deliberate erasure of the Amarna kings from the official record, matching the dismantling of their monuments. Their reigns are well attested elsewhere, so the omission is ideological, not an accident.

questions.stem: Which statement best describes the long-term consequences of the Amarna Period by 1292 BCE?
options: the Aten remained Egypt's chief god until the end of the New Kingdom
Akhetaten remained the capital, and Thebes was left to the priests
the priesthood of Amun was permanently abolished and its lands given to the crown
the old religion was restored and the Amarna kings were written out of history
questions.explanation: Under Tutankhamun, Ay and Horemheb, Amun and the other gods were restored, Akhetaten was abandoned and its kings erased from king lists. The Amun priesthood regained its wealth, so the crisis ended largely in a return to the old order.
